subtitle: Carry equity considerations through every stage of organizational change. Start with the reason for the change and the decision itself, then follow through to implementation and a review of the actual result.
scope: For DHS leaders working on organizational, policy, service or workforce changes. Practice planning routines support analysis and implementation; they do not replace the formal DHS equity-analysis requirement or delegate budget, labor, legal, procurement or policy authority.
introTranscript: Organizational change can improve a service and still create new barriers along the way. A faster process may shift work to people with less time, reduce a useful route for questions or leave staff without the preparation to use it. This course follows a practice DHS intake redesign from an initial problem to implementation and review. You will distinguish a meaningful outcome from a new chart or procedure, include relevant perspectives, connect the analysis to an authorized decision and make follow-through visible. One DSD provides learning and practical support under the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant’s direction. Staff retain responsibility for doing their work; consultation adds guidance and feedback. Actual changes still use the appropriate DHS procedures and decision authority.

lessons.title: Define the change by the result people need
lessons.summary: A proposed structure or tool is a means. Start with the actual problem, affected tasks and intended improvement.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a proposed method from a meaningful outcome.
objectives: Distinguish a proposed method from a meaningful outcome.
Describe an equity-relevant change problem without claiming a cause from incomplete data.
Connect a long-term action to the actual DHS equity-analysis process.
takeaways: Name the problem before choosing the method.
Describe the affected people and tasks with evidence and limits.
A course reflection does not replace a required formal analysis.
lessons.statement: A new procedure is not the outcome. The outcome is what improves for people using the work or service.

image.caption: A clear problem statement gives the change discussion a shared purpose.

intro.heading: Make the purpose concrete
intro.body:
A DHS team proposes replacing several intake contacts with one digital entry point. The project summary says “modernize intake.” That explains a direction but not the problem or the intended result. Which people cannot obtain timely information now? Which steps are repeated? Does the proposal address those issues, or simply move the complexity to a different place?

Start with a concrete task and relevant evidence. A useful statement might describe people waiting for a response, staff repeating data entry or confusion about the next contact. If figures differ across groups, examine the measure, period, completeness and context before attributing a cause. The evidence may identify a difference worth investigating without proving why it occurs. Staff and community experience can help explain questions the counts do not answer, but one account does not establish every person’s experience.

Define the intended result in terms people can use: clearer next steps, fewer unnecessary repetitions or an effective response through the available route. “Launch the portal” describes an output. “People can complete the necessary intake step without losing access to support” describes a task outcome that needs evidence. Both can be useful, but should not be confused.

DHS Equity Policy requires equity considerations across work and specifies a formal analysis for actions with prolonged or long-term impact scheduled for the stated approvals. Use the DHS Equity Analysis or Equity Scan within the required Toolkit, or a customized tool developed in consultation with an equity director under the policy. This course’s short planning exercise is preparation, not proof that the requirement has been fulfilled.

A leader can ask the responsible team to state the problem, intended result, available evidence and major uncertainty before defending a preferred solution. That makes the change easier to examine and gives the authorized decision a clearer basis.

inThisLesson: Separate a method from an outcome.
Describe the task and available evidence.
Use the formal analysis route when required.
lessons.keyStatement: State what should improve for people and how you will know, not only what the team will launch.

flashcards.back: A proposed tool, structure or procedure. It is a way of pursuing an outcome, not proof that the outcome has been achieved.
The meaningful result for the affected work or people. It needs a definition and appropriate evidence rather than a completion label.
A concrete description of the task, barrier and available evidence. It should separate supported facts from assumptions about cause.
The analysis required under the actual DHS policy using its Toolkit or qualifying customized tool. A course exercise does not satisfy it automatically.

items.title: Ask what the present process does
items.body: Map the actual intake steps, handoffs and information people need. An organizational chart may not reveal the point at which someone loses the path. Include the informal support staff currently provide so it is not accidentally removed.

items.title: Test the claim about improvement
items.body: A single entry point may reduce repetition but could create a new digital barrier. State the expected mechanism and the evidence needed to examine it. Do not assume that a newer tool or a shorter process helps every person in the same way.

items.title: Keep requirements distinct
items.body: The learning worksheet can prepare questions. Formal policy analysis, accessibility review and decision authority still have their own requirements. Identify those routes early rather than treating a completed worksheet as authorization.

tabs.label: Output
tabs.body: “The new portal was released” describes delivery. In the practice redesign, that fact can be confirmed by a release record even if the instructions still leave someone unsure which contact answers a question. Delivery matters because the intended change cannot be examined until it exists. It is nevertheless a different claim from effective access. Record the release as an output, then ask for evidence about the necessary intake task rather than using the launch date as the answer to both questions.

tabs.label: Task outcome
tabs.body: “The tested intake path supports completion and a clear response” describes a task result. A useful account says which steps were tested, who participated, what support was available and what remained unexamined. For example, a test using prepared documents and available assistance may support a finding about that route; it does not establish how an unsupported first-time user will fare. The scope makes the finding usable: it shows what the team can reasonably carry forward and what still needs evidence.

tabs.label: Unsupported cause
tabs.body: “Any difference must be caused by lack of interest” assigns a motive the figures cannot establish. In the practice redesign, a difference in completion could warrant questions about instructions, available help, technology or the circumstances of the task. Those are possible explanations to examine, not findings to substitute for the first assumption. Ask what evidence could distinguish them. This changes the next action from blaming people to investigating the path while keeping the actual cause uncertain.

check.question: Which statement best defines the intended change outcome?
check.correct: People can complete the necessary intake step with clear information and effective access; the team will examine that result with appropriate evidence.
wrong: The team launches a new portal, so every access problem is solved.
A shorter organizational chart proves the service is equitable.
The course worksheet automatically fulfills the required DHS Toolkit analysis.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This defines the task result and leaves room for verification. Delivery and a formal policy requirement remain distinct questions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A portal release establishes delivery, not that every access problem is resolved; the necessary task still needs examination. A shorter organizational chart describes structure and cannot prove people can complete intake or receive a clear response. The course worksheet can help you prepare your thinking, but it does not automatically satisfy the required DHS Toolkit or appropriately consulted customized-tool analysis. Define the intended task result, identify evidence for it and keep the actual policy process separate from optional practice.

items.text: People receive a clear next contact after intake.
The team releases a new online entry point.
Launching the tool proves every group benefits equally.
Staff avoid unnecessary duplicate entry in the tested process.
Three teams are combined into one unit.
A brief reflection replaces every formal analysis requirement.

lessons.next: Next, examine the people and perspectives needed before the preferred solution hardens.

scenario.context: A practice leader describes success only as launching a new intake tool by a date. Staff report that some people may lose the existing question route, but the project note does not mention it.
options: A concrete task outcome, the affected support route, relevant evidence and the required analysis questions before the authorized decision.
A more attractive launch announcement only.
A claim that every concern is resistance to change.
responses: This makes the intended benefit and potential barrier examinable. It does not prejudge whether the tool should be adopted.
An announcement cannot supply missing evidence or protect a route the design has overlooked.
Concern can contain useful task information. Do not assign motive before examining it.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice change statement with the task problem, intended result, proposed method and one uncertainty requiring analysis.

move.control: You can clarify the purpose before defending a solution.
move.failure: Delivery is presented as proof of equitable outcomes.
move.next: Define the task result and use the required analysis and decision routes.

lessons.title: Bring relevant perspectives into the design
lessons.summary: Participation is useful when it can influence the questions and options. Attendance alone does not establish meaningful involvement.
lessons.objective: Identify a missing work or community perspective relevant to a change.
objectives: Identify a missing work or community perspective relevant to a change.
Distinguish consultation input from authority to decide.
Plan an accessible feedback loop explaining what happened to the input.
takeaways: Ask who experiences the proposed change and who has not been heard.
Input can shape options without transferring formal authority.
Explain how concerns were considered and what remains unresolved.
lessons.statement: A listening activity matters when people can see how their information entered the work.

image.caption: Different perspectives can reveal an overlooked task without being treated as a single group voice.

intro.heading: Listen before the choices are fixed
intro.body:
The practice intake project invites staff after the design is already selected. They can comment on the colors but not the loss of a support route. This is participation with a narrow scope. Be honest about what is open, what is already decided and who has authority. Do not call a constrained feedback activity shared decision-making when it is not.

DHS Equity Policy emphasizes meaningful ongoing community engagement and equity consideration in internal and external work. GAO’s transformation guidance also discusses employee involvement and two-way communication. These sources support a practical question: what experience or knowledge is needed to understand the proposed change, and how will that information influence the work? They do not make every participant an authorized policy approver.

Look for task perspectives rather than a token representative for an entire identity group. Frontline staff may know repeated handoff problems. People using the service may describe an inaccessible instruction or an unanswered question. Technical and legal colleagues may identify requirements that a proposal has missed. One person’s account is valuable without becoming the voice of every person with a similar background.

Make participation usable: clear questions, appropriate language and disability access, relevant material and a safe way to provide input through the actual agency process. Do not request private health or recipient information merely to make a story persuasive. Any actual confidential records, compensation, public engagement or formal consultation obligations need their authorized handling. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA under the owner’s direction; this course does not teach that specialized process.

Close the loop by explaining which concerns changed the option, which remain uncertain and which cannot be acted on within the stated authority. Do not promise that every suggestion will be adopted. A respectful explanation makes both the influence and the limit visible.

inThisLesson: State the scope and authority honestly.
Explain how input influenced the work.
lessons.keyStatement: Participation should inform the work; it should not be overstated as consent, representation or approval.

flashcards.back: Experience or expertise that helps examine the change. A participant is not automatically the representative of every person sharing an identity or role.
A matter the process can still influence. Stating it honestly helps participants use their time meaningfully.
The actual role authorized to decide a policy, budget or work change. Receiving input does not transfer or remove that authority.
An explanation of how input was considered, what changed and what remains unresolved. It is not a promise to adopt every suggestion.

items.title: Invite the missing task knowledge
items.body: Ask who sees the step the design team does not. A receptionist, analyst or service user may describe a handoff that is absent from the flowchart. Invite that knowledge before assuming the chart captures the full experience.

items.title: Give a clear scope
items.body: Explain whether the group is identifying barriers, comparing options or commenting on implementation. If some decisions are fixed, state that. Do not invite an open-ended conversation and later reveal that only visual details were open.

items.title: Show the effect of input
items.body: Record the concern in appropriately protected form and connect it to a design question or decision explanation. Participation without a visible response can leave people unsure whether the issue was understood, even when the team did useful work.

tabs.label: Individual account
tabs.body: A service user describes being unsure where to ask about the new intake step. That account is evidence of the experience described and can identify a part of the route worth examining. It is not a count of everyone with that experience. Clarify the step and the account’s context without requesting unnecessary private information, then examine the relevant instruction and response route. If there is a current unmet need, help connect it to the appropriate timely response; a broader design inquiry is a separate task.

tabs.label: Pattern across sources
tabs.body: Suppose a staff observation, a scoped task test and several user accounts each identify confusion at the same handoff. Their agreement can strengthen the reason to examine that handoff when they concern the same route and period. Repeated copies of one account are not independent sources, and accounts about different routes may describe different problems. Explain the connection and remaining limits. This helps the team direct its inquiry without presenting the number of comments as a representative rate or proof of cause.

tabs.label: Formal decision
tabs.body: The input may support retaining a help route, while cost, policy and implementation questions still require the actual authorized decision. A feedback meeting can develop the recommendation and explain what matters to participants; attendance does not grant contract or policy authority. The responsible decision should consider applicable requirements and relevant evidence and explain how the input informed the choice. That can include a choice remaining unchanged with reasons. The distinction protects both meaningful participation and an honest account of who decides.

check.question: A staff listening session identifies a barrier. What can the team accurately say?
check.correct: The session provides relevant input to examine; explain its scope and how it informs the authorized design and decision process.
wrong: The session proves every affected person agrees.
The most outspoken participant represents every member of their group.
The session automatically replaces all formal review and approval requirements.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Input is substantive without being overstated as total consent or authority. It should influence the appropriate question and receive a clear response.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Participation in one listening session does not establish that every affected person agrees; say whose input was available and what it can support. An outspoken participant can describe their own knowledge or experience but does not automatically represent an entire group. A session also cannot replace applicable formal review or authorized approval. Use the barrier account to examine the relevant task, explain how it informs the recommendation and keep the real decision process visible.

items.text: Frontline staff identify an overlooked handoff.
The team explains which options remain open.
Attendance means everyone consented to the final change.
A service user describes a confusing instruction.
The decision note explains why one concern changed the proposed route.
One participant speaks for an entire identity group.

lessons.next: Next, compare options and burdens rather than using feedback only to decorate the preferred solution.

scenario.context: A practice project team hears that an online-only route may block some users. The leader thanks participants but removes the concern from the record because it would complicate the launch story.
options: Preserve the concern appropriately, examine the task and options, and explain its influence or unresolved status in the authorized decision.
Treat the concern as proof that every digital tool must be rejected.
responses: Selective recording hides information needed for a sound decision. Respectful listening includes substantive follow-through.
This keeps the work open to relevant evidence without predetermining the outcome. Protect personal information and use the proper review route.
A concern identifies a question; it does not automatically settle every option. Examine the actual barrier and requirements.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a practice participation plan with a missing perspective, an open question, an accessible input route and how the team will explain its response.

move.control: You can make input useful and scope honest.
move.failure: Consultation is treated as decoration or universal consent.
move.next: Connect relevant perspectives to actual options and explain the effect on the work.

lessons.title: Compare benefits, burdens and implementation needs
lessons.summary: An option can improve one part of the work while shifting effort or risk elsewhere. Make the tradeoffs and missing evidence visible.
lessons.objective: Identify a burden shifted by a proposed change.
objectives: Identify a burden shifted by a proposed change.
Compare options using the same task and relevant evidence.
Distinguish an uncertain benefit from a supported finding and a non-negotiable requirement.
takeaways: Do not examine the benefit without the burden.
Compare options on a common task and context.
A promised future result is not a verified finding.
lessons.statement: A faster step is not necessarily a better complete path if the effort is simply moved to someone else.

image.caption: A comparison should show who gains, who does more work and what remains uncertain.

intro.heading: Examine the whole path
intro.body:
The practice intake team compares an online-only option with a supported digital route that retains help for people who need it. The online-only option may reduce some staff contacts. It may also require users to resolve confusing instructions or technical problems without assistance. Those effects should be examined, not assumed. The question is how the complete path works for affected people and staff.

Use a consistent comparison. Describe the same necessary task, time period and service context for each option. Identify expected benefits, possible burdens, relevant requirements, cost or capacity questions and evidence still needed. A practice comparison table can help organize the discussion, but an invented numerical equity score cannot certify the policy or replace the formal analysis.

Ask where work moves. A change may shift data entry from staff to users, support work from a central team to frontline staff or coordination effort to another division. That can be appropriate in some circumstances, but the proposal should show the capacity, information and access needed. An unplanned shift can appear efficient in one unit’s measure while making the agency’s overall task harder.

Separate requirements from preferences and estimates. Accessibility, legal authority and actual policy obligations cannot be waived because a preferred option has a promising average time. Procurement, budget, labor and service changes use their appropriate routes. Predicted benefits need explicit assumptions and later review; they are not current results.

Prepare a recommendation that states the reasoning, uncertainty and conditions needed for implementation. The leader can propose a supported option and identify the next evidence or authorized decision. This is more useful than declaring one option equitable because it is popular, technologically new or cheapest in a narrow spreadsheet.

inThisLesson: State a supported recommendation with limits.
lessons.keyStatement: Show what changes for people and the assumptions behind the expected benefit.

flashcards.back: Work, time or risk moved from one person or unit to another. Examine it in the complete task rather than only the proposing unit’s measure.
Options examined using the same relevant task, context and definitions. A mismatched comparison can create a misleading advantage.
A proposed future improvement supported by assumptions. It is distinct from a result already observed after implementation.
A requirement or supported prerequisite that must be addressed through the authorized process before or during implementation. A course table does not waive it.

items.title: Look for the uncounted step
items.body: The new form may be faster to process while users spend longer finding missing information. Ask whether the measure captures the whole task or only one team’s step. Do not assume the uncounted effort is trivial.

items.title: Describe uncertainty clearly
items.body: A small practice test may suggest a benefit, but may not represent every group or real service context. Record the limitations and the evidence needed. Unknown impact should not be labeled no impact.

items.title: Separate the recommendation from authority
items.body: A staff analysis can recommend an option with reasons and safeguards. Actual approval, funding or contract changes remain with authorized roles. Do not imply that a well-written report grants powers the author does not have.

tabs.label: Reasoning
tabs.body: In the practice comparison, the supported digital route is recommended because users can obtain clarification at a necessary step, not merely because its demonstration looked attractive. Connect that reasoning to the evidence available: a limited task test, a documented support route or a specific unresolved problem. Explain where an expected benefit still depends on an assumption. A reader can then examine the connection between problem and option instead of having to accept the team’s enthusiasm as evidence.

tabs.label: Tradeoff
tabs.body: Keeping help available may require staff time even while the digital form reduces another task. Name that resource question and who would experience the work; neither ignoring it nor calling it automatically unacceptable produces a useful comparison. Examine the whole path, available capacity and relevant requirements. A tradeoff may lead to a different arrangement or a supported condition rather than rejection of the entire option. This makes the recommendation practical without treating a person’s access as a discretionary cost to dismiss.

tabs.label: Condition and review
tabs.body: If the recommendation depends on another unit answering help requests, the plan needs an actual agreement, capacity and a usable route rather than an assumed promise. Identify who handles that arrangement and what evidence will show it is ready. Later review can examine whether the support and intended result worked. It cannot postpone a current required accessibility, privacy or other safeguard until after harm occurs. A condition is a concrete prerequisite or review action through real authority, not a sentence that makes an unresolved requirement disappear.

check.question: An option lowers one unit’s processing time but adds unmeasured user effort. What should the analysis do?
check.correct: Examine the complete task, the shifted burden and missing evidence before making a supported recommendation.
wrong: Declare the option equitable from the unit’s faster average alone.
Treat every shifted task as automatically prohibited.
Assign a made-up equity score and treat it as formal approval.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The efficiency measure is useful within its scope, but the uncounted burden matters. The analysis should compare actual options and requirements rather than use an automatic rule.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The unit’s faster average measures one part of the work and leaves the added user effort unresolved, so it cannot alone establish an equitable complete path. A shifted task is not automatically prohibited; examine the burden, capacity, access and applicable requirements rather than assuming every change is unacceptable. An invented equity score grants no formal approval and may hide unsupported assumptions. Compare the real options on the same complete task, state the uncertainty and use the authorized process.

items.text: The timed test covered only the staff processing step.
Users are expected to resolve technical errors without help.
Cheapest automatically means most equitable.
The current route includes a support contact people use.
The proposal assumes another unit has capacity for the new handoff.
A practice score grants policy approval authority.

lessons.next: Next, turn the chosen direction into work people can actually carry out.

scenario.context: A practice leader recommends a redesign using an average processing time from one small test. The recommendation says there are no risks because the support route was not measured.
options: Keep the claim because the measured average improved.
Discard every test result because it is not complete.
Retain the scoped finding, identify the unmeasured support and access questions, and state the conditions and further evidence needed.
responses: Not measured does not mean no risk. The complete task remains to be examined.
The test can provide useful limited evidence. Its limits should be stated rather than used as a reason to ignore it.
This uses the evidence honestly and supports a more complete recommendation. Formal requirements still apply now, not only at a later review.

lessons.transfer: Compare two practice options using the task result, shifted burden, requirement, assumption and evidence needed. Do not create a certification score.

move.control: You can make tradeoffs and uncertainty visible.
move.failure: A narrow efficiency measure hides work shifted to others.
move.next: Compare the complete path and attach conditions to the supported recommendation.

lessons.title: Make implementation roles and capacity real
lessons.summary: A decision needs responsible work, preparation and resources. An owner without authority or time is not a complete implementation plan.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a named task owner from a role authorized to decide.
objectives: Distinguish a named task owner from a role authorized to decide.
Identify a capacity or dependency gap in an implementation plan.
Connect learning and preparation to actual changed duties.
takeaways: Name who acts, who decides and who supports.
Check time, tools and dependencies rather than assigning work by label.
Training should prepare the real task and does not replace all other requirements.
lessons.statement: Responsibility becomes useful when the person has the means and authority appropriate to the work.

image.caption: An implementation note should connect the action to the people and resources needed to deliver it.

intro.heading: Move beyond assigning names
intro.body:
The practice intake redesign is approved through the actual agency process. The plan assigns a staff member to update instructions, train colleagues, configure the tool and monitor results. That is a list of expectations, not necessarily a workable plan. Which tasks are within the staff member’s role? Which need technical, accessibility or procurement support? What existing work must be adjusted to make time?

GAO’s transformation guidance discusses implementation responsibility, sequencing, communication and resources. Use those general practices as planning support rather than treating an old federal report as Minnesota’s required organizational structure. A small change may not need a new committee. It does need clear responsibility and a route for decisions that exceed the work owner’s authority.

Distinguish the person doing a task, the role authorized to decide and those providing necessary expertise or support. An analyst can prepare evidence without approving a policy. A supervisor can coordinate preparation without signing a procurement amendment. The consultant provides program leadership, guidance and feedback; staff retain the work responsibility appropriate to their roles.

Check dependencies. If instructions depend on an unfinished configuration, the training date may be premature. If another unit must accept a handoff, its capacity and agreement cannot be assumed. Digital tools and content need the applicable accessibility process. Labor, privacy, budget and other formal questions use their responsible routes.

Preparation should match the changed task. Give people usable instructions, relevant practice, a way to raise problems and an accurate account of what is changing. Course completion can support learning but does not itself prove competence in every task or satisfy every separate DHS training obligation. For the practice exercise, create a small implementation note with action, owner, decision route, resources, dependency and evidence of readiness. It helps the team see an unworkable promise before the deadline arrives.

inThisLesson: Make escalation and support routes clear.
lessons.keyStatement: A named owner is only part of the plan; authority, capacity and dependencies still need attention.

flashcards.back: The person or unit responsible for doing an action through the real work process. Ownership does not automatically grant budget, policy or contract authority.
The role and process used when an approval, unresolved limit or formal question needs a decision. Name it accurately rather than inventing a new authority.
Something another action needs first, such as a usable configuration or another unit’s readiness. An assumed dependency can undermine the implementation schedule.
Evidence that the task, supports and necessary arrangements are available. A date on a plan or training attendance alone does not establish readiness.

items.title: Authority
items.body: What can the owner decide, and what must be referred? A person may be accountable for preparation without being the approver. State the distinction so unresolved decisions do not stay hidden as missed tasks.

items.title: Capacity
items.body: What time, tools and specialist support are needed? Adding a large change assignment to unchanged duties can create a predictable bottleneck. Examine the work and use the actual management and resource process.

items.title: Dependencies
items.body: What needs to be ready before this action works? A training session on an unstable screen can teach a process that changes immediately. Coordinate sequencing and state what remains unfinished.

tabs.label: Assigned
tabs.body: Putting an analyst’s name beside “configure the intake tool” records an expectation. It does not establish permission to alter the vendor system, time to do the work or a specialist’s availability. Check what the analyst can do and which action needs another role. Otherwise, a delay may be treated as an individual failure when the missing decision is elsewhere. Keep the owner named, but separate their preparation task from the authorized configuration or contract decision so the plan can be carried out.

tabs.label: Prepared
tabs.body: The team has usable instructions, relevant practice and support for the changed task. Examine them together: if practice uses an unfinished screen, staff may learn a sequence that no longer matches the released tool. A rehearsal of the actual task can identify a missing instruction or handoff, with its scope stated honestly. Preparation also needs the applicable reviews and arrangements; a good practice session does not waive them. The point is to establish a usable way of working, not merely a completed training event.

tabs.label: Ready to proceed
tabs.body: The responsible process has considered the necessary conditions and made the appropriate decision. For the practice intake route, that might include a stable configuration, usable instructions, a support arrangement and completed applicable reviews; the actual requirements determine the list. State any remaining limits accurately. A launch date or attendance list alone does not establish this state. Distinguishing readiness from assignment and preparation helps the leader see which decision is still needed instead of compressing all three into a single “done” label.

check.question: A plan names a staff owner but gives no time, technical support or route for approvals. What is missing?
check.correct: A workable account of capacity, dependencies and decision authority for the actual tasks.
wrong: Nothing; a name establishes every needed resource.
A new committee is legally required for every change.
The staff member can approve any purchase because they own implementation.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Ownership is important but incomplete. The plan needs the means and proper authority for the work without inventing a mandatory structure or delegated powers.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A name beside an action does not provide time, specialist support or permission to change a contract. A new committee is not shown to be legally required for every change by the planning guidance; use proportionate coordination and the actual agency requirements. Owning implementation also does not give the staff member purchasing authority. Identify the preparation task, required decision, resources and dependency separately so the assignment is workable without inventing powers or structures.

items.text: Who may approve the required contract change?
Is the final configuration ready before staff practice?
A named owner can authorize every needed expense.
Which role decides an unresolved policy question?
What existing workload makes room for the new action?
A launch date proves all conditions are ready.

lessons.next: Next, communicate the change while making room for questions and correction.

scenario.context: A practice analyst is assigned to implement a new intake route but cannot change the vendor configuration or approve the required terms. The leader calls the delay a commitment problem.
options: The authority and dependency gaps, required specialist actions and realistic work capacity before assigning a character judgment.
Whether public criticism will create procurement authority.
Whether all specialist review can be skipped because the deadline is close.
responses: This uses the actual work facts and can make the plan feasible. A delay does not establish lack of commitment when needed decisions are outside the owner’s role.
Pressure does not grant authority. Identify the actual decision route.
A deadline does not remove formal responsibilities. Sequence the work and use the authorized process.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a practice implementation row with action, owner, authority route, capacity, dependency and evidence needed for readiness.

move.failure: An owner is blamed for decisions and resources outside their role.
move.next: Clarify authority, arrange support and review the actual dependency before judging progress.

lessons.title: Communicate change and respond to useful concern
lessons.summary: Clear information and two-way response help people understand what changes, what stays and how problems can influence implementation.
lessons.objective: Write a change message stating the purpose, actual change and next action.
objectives: Write a change message stating the purpose, actual change and next action.
Distinguish a relevant concern from an unsupported judgment that all disagreement is resistance.
Plan a response route for urgent barriers and ordinary implementation questions.
takeaways: State the purpose and concrete work change.
Ask what a concern reveals about the task or evidence.
A feedback route needs an owner and response, not merely an inbox.
lessons.statement: People should not have to infer the change from a slogan or guess whether their concern has a route.

image.caption: A useful change message prepares people for the work and explains where questions go.

intro.heading: Make the next step understandable
intro.body:
The practice intake project announces “a new era of streamlined service.” Staff still do not know which contact changes, when the change applies or what to do if the new route fails. A polished slogan is not an implementation message. State the purpose, the actual work change, effective arrangement, responsibilities and where questions can be raised through the real process. Avoid promising benefits that are still assumptions.

GAO’s guidance emphasizes early, consistent and two-way communication. In this course, that means the leader both explains and listens. A concern may reveal a missing instruction, a capacity gap, a legal requirement or an access barrier. It may also be based on a misunderstanding. Examine the content rather than treating every concern as resistance or every suggestion as a command to reverse the decision.

Use plain language and usable formats. Distinguish what is decided from what remains open, and say who owns the next answer. Different audiences may need different detail: staff need work instructions; people using the service need a clear route and what it means for them. Keep the underlying facts consistent and use the actual language and disability-access arrangements. Do not disclose private case or staff information merely to explain why a change occurred.

A feedback route needs follow-through. Identify who reads it, what kind of issue belongs there and how it connects to the right owner. Urgent safety, rights, privacy or other formal matters must not wait in a general improvement inbox when immediate or specialized action is required. A listening process cannot replace reporting or complaint duties.

For the practice exercise, draft a short message and a response plan. State the evidence for the expected benefit, one unresolved question and the route for a practical barrier. The aim is informed implementation, not unanimous enthusiasm or a claim that communication alone makes the change sound.

inThisLesson: Keep decisions and open questions distinct.
Provide responsible response and formal routes.
lessons.keyStatement: A clear message and a functioning response route are part of implementation, not proof that every concern is resolved.

flashcards.back: A practical account of the purpose, actual work change and next action. It should not rely only on promotional language.
A question or observation that may affect the work. Examine its content before assigning motive or assuming it decides the outcome.
The actual owner and process for receiving and acting on questions. An inbox without responsibility can leave barriers unattended.
A safety, rights, privacy, employment or other issue requiring its proper process. A general change-feedback channel does not replace it.

items.title: Say what is changing
items.body: Name the step, owner or instruction rather than only the program’s ambition. Include what people need to do next and where current information lives. If the arrangement is pending, say so accurately.

items.title: State what remains open
items.body: Some questions may concern implementation while the policy direction is already authorized. Explain the scope honestly. Do not invite an apparently open decision and later dismiss all input because it was never in scope.

items.title: Respond to the substance
items.body: A worried staff member may know a task problem the project missed. Clarify the observation and evidence. Respectful examination neither requires agreeing with every claim nor permits dismissing all concern as a character flaw.

tabs.label: Work question
tabs.body: A staff member asks which contact now handles an intake question because two instructions point to different teams. Clarify the actual arrangement with its responsible owner and correct the shared material through the proper process. This may be an instruction problem rather than evidence that the whole redesign should be reversed. A clear answer reduces the need for people to reconstruct the route independently. If the arrangement itself is unresolved, say so and identify the next responsible action rather than supplying a guessed contact.

tabs.label: Design concern
tabs.body: Before implementation, a service user asks whether the proposed handoff would remove a language-help route. Examine the prospective task effect and connect the concern to the responsible design and access review. This can reveal an assumption missing from the proposal even if no current loss has occurred. Keep that future design question distinct from an actual unmet access need, which retains its timely appropriate response. The design-feedback process should improve the proposal without becoming a waiting queue for help someone needs now.

tabs.label: Urgent or formal issue
tabs.body: A reported confidential-record exposure is not merely another suggestion for the next project meeting. Use the actual privacy or incident route promptly and share information only as appropriate to that process. The implementation team can separately examine a resulting process correction when authorized. This separation matters because the ordinary feedback schedule may be suitable for a proposed improvement but unsuitable for a current protection or reporting duty. Neither broad publication nor silence is a substitute for the proper response.

check.question: A staff member raises a concern about an intake handoff during implementation. What is the useful first response?
check.correct: Clarify the task observation and evidence, then connect it to the responsible response or formal route rather than assuming resistance.
wrong: Label the staff member resistant before examining the issue.
Promise to adopt every suggestion immediately.
Keep all urgent matters in a monthly general feedback queue.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The content may reveal a barrier or misunderstanding. Examine it and use the right route without an automatic character judgment or unsupported promise.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Calling the person resistant before examining the handoff can hide a missing instruction or barrier; clarify the task observation first. Promising immediate adoption of every suggestion ignores evidence, other effects and actual decision authority; explain the review and response instead. Placing every urgent matter in a monthly queue can delay a required privacy, safety or other formal response. The issue’s substance determines the proper route, while ordinary implementation feedback can retain its proportionate review process.

items.text: A staff member cannot identify the new contact from the instructions.

Before implementation, a service user describes a possible loss of language help under the proposed handoff. This is a future design risk; any current unmet need retains its timely appropriate access response.
The new process exposes confidential records.
The meeting leaves the next responsible action unclear.
A unit reports that the proposed handoff exceeds its available capacity.
A current safety concern needs immediate agency response.

lessons.next: The final lesson reviews actual results and makes supported correction part of the change.

scenario.context: A practice change mailbox receives a report of a possible confidential-data exposure. The project lead wants to wait for the monthly improvement meeting.
options: Wait, because every change issue follows the same queue.
Route the concern promptly through the actual privacy and incident process while preserving appropriate information and the separate implementation follow-up.
Publish the report broadly to demonstrate transparency.
responses: A routine improvement schedule does not replace formal or urgent duties. The actual issue determines the proper route.
This keeps the specialized response timely and lets the implementation owner address any related process finding without exposing unnecessary details.
Transparency does not authorize public disclosure of confidential records. Use the actual process.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice change message stating purpose, concrete action, open question and response owner, with a separate route for a formal urgent issue.

move.control: You can explain the work and examine concerns.
move.failure: Slogans or resistance labels replace usable communication.
move.next: State the next action clearly and connect each issue to its appropriate response.

lessons.title: Review the result and make supported correction
lessons.summary: Implementation completion is not the same as an equitable result. Review the promised outcome, unintended effects and limits of the evidence.
lessons.objective: Distinguish implementation activity from outcome evidence.
objectives: Distinguish implementation activity from outcome evidence.
Interpret a before-and-after change without assuming causation.
Prepare a supported continuation, adjustment or referral through the authorized process.
takeaways: Compare the observed result with the stated purpose.
Check missing information and unintended effects.
Use review findings to inform the authorized next action.
lessons.statement: Follow-through asks what actually changed for people, not only whether the project list is complete.

image.caption: A review can acknowledge useful progress and remaining barriers in the same account.

intro.heading: Use evidence to keep improving the change
intro.body:
The practice intake redesign is live. The project reports that processing time decreased and all staff attended training. Those are useful facts, but they answer different questions. The processing measure needs its definition, period and context. Training attendance describes an activity, not whether staff can perform the changed task or people can obtain effective access. Return to the intended result stated at the beginning.

Compare the relevant evidence carefully. A before-and-after difference does not prove the redesign caused it; workload, case mix, recording or other conditions may have changed. Check whether measures are comparable and whether missing data, small groups or changed reporting limit interpretation. Protect confidential information and avoid publishing identifying group details. Unknown results should not be presented as no concerns.

Review unintended effects and who experiences them. A faster central step may coincide with more unresolved questions elsewhere. Staff and service-user perspectives can reveal issues needing further examination. Use those accounts with appropriate context rather than treating one story as a universal outcome or dismissing it because the average improved.

A supported review may recommend continuing the approach, adjusting a part, gathering more evidence or referring a formal issue. The actual authority and requirements still govern the decision. A test or pilot does not create an exemption from rights, policy or reporting obligations. If a current serious barrier exists, respond through the appropriate process rather than waiting for a later learning review.

Record the finding, uncertainty, next action, responsible owner and review arrangement. Where relevant, connect the result to the ADSA implementation goals and the division’s actual work process, not just a decorative label. The consultant can provide guidance and feedback while staff do their analysis and follow-through. This completes a learning cycle without declaring the organization equitable from one successful project.

inThisLesson: Recommend the next action through actual authority.
lessons.keyStatement: A complete project can still have unresolved outcomes; name both progress and remaining work.

flashcards.back: Evidence of work performed, such as training or launch. It does not automatically establish task access or equitable outcomes.
Information about the actual result, with definitions, context and limitations. Keep it distinct from an administrative completion status.
A change in figures may have several explanations. A before-and-after observation alone does not establish the redesign as the cause.
An action grounded in relevant findings and taken through the authorized process. It is not a reflexive reversal or an informal policy waiver.

items.title: Examine the promised outcome
items.body: If the promise was clear next steps, ask whether people received and could use them. A release date or lower processing time may be relevant, but cannot substitute for every part of that outcome.

items.title: Keep missing evidence visible
items.body: If a group’s result is unmeasured or too limited to report safely, state the limit and plan appropriate evidence. Do not treat absence of figures as reassurance or expose small identifiable counts to make the chart complete.

items.title: Connect the next action
items.body: A finding is useful when someone can act on it. Name the responsible work owner, actual decision route and what will be checked next. Do not invent an approval from the learning review itself.

tabs.heading: Different next steps can be responsible

tabs.label: Continue
tabs.body: Relevant evidence supports keeping the intake route within actual requirements, while stated limits and ongoing support remain visible. For example, a scoped test may show that the revised instruction resolves the examined handoff; it does not establish permanent success for every future user or change. Identify what will continue to be checked and who owns that work. Continuation preserves a supported improvement without closing the response route to a later barrier or treating a successful project as proof about the entire organization.

tabs.label: Adjust
tabs.body: A recurring unclear handoff may call for correcting the instruction or responsibility at that step rather than replacing the entire digital route. Confirm the task evidence, use the appropriate authority and examine whether the correction addresses the identified problem. Other findings may justify a larger change, but the scale should follow the evidence and requirements. A proportionate adjustment makes follow-through specific: it identifies what will change, who can arrange it and what result will be reviewed, instead of turning every concern into an automatic total verdict.

tabs.label: Investigate or refer
tabs.body: If the support outcome was not measured, the team can describe that uncertainty and plan appropriate evidence rather than labeling the result favorable. If a report concerns a current serious barrier or formal matter, connect it promptly to the actual specialist or response process while keeping any broader review separate. These are different next steps: further inquiry develops knowledge, and a required response addresses the present issue. Neither the word “investigate” nor a future review date authorizes delaying current protection or reporting duties.

check.question: After launch, processing time improves while one support route remains unmeasured. What is the accurate conclusion?
check.correct: The measured result improved within its stated context, while the support outcome remains unresolved and needs appropriate examination.
wrong: Every outcome is equitable because the average improved.
The redesign certainly caused the difference with no other explanation.
Missing support data proves there is no barrier.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This uses the finding without overstating it. Context, comparability, causal limits and the unmeasured part remain relevant to the next decision.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An improved average does not establish every outcome or every group’s experience; the unmeasured support route remains a separate question. A before-and-after difference alone also cannot establish that the redesign caused it, because context, recording or case mix may differ. Missing support figures provide no evidence that a barrier is absent. Retain the useful measured finding within its scope, state the causal and outcome limits and connect the unresolved question or current concern to its appropriate next action.

items.text: The measured processing interval decreased in the stated period.
The support route’s result has not been examined.
Launch proves all affected groups benefited equally.
The corrected instruction worked in the described task test.
A change in case mix may affect the before-and-after comparison.
No figures mean there were no concerns.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to carry a practice change from purpose through review. Actual changes still use the DHS analysis, decision and implementation processes.

scenario.context: A practice project closes after training and launch. Staff report a recurring unclear handoff, but the leader says completion means there is nothing left to review.
scenario.prompt: What is the stronger next step?
options: Close every concern because the project list is complete.
Treat the reports as proof that the entire change failed without examining them.
Review the actual handoff and outcome evidence, respond through the proper process and assign supported correction or further inquiry.
responses: Administrative completion does not settle the outcome or current barrier.
The reports identify useful questions. Examine the task and context before declaring a total verdict.
This preserves progress while making follow-through real. Use actual authority and do not delay urgent or formal responses.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a practice review note with one supported result, one uncertainty, one unintended effect question and the responsible next action.

move.control: You can keep outcomes and correction visible after launch.
move.failure: Project completion becomes a permanent equity claim.
move.next: Compare the actual task result with the purpose and use supported findings for authorized follow-through.

jobAid.subtitle: Carry equity through an organizational change
remember: Define the meaningful result before defending a method.
Use the formal DHS analysis process when required.
Participation informs the work without becoming automatic approval.
Implementation and outcome evidence answer different questions.

sections.heading: Examine the proposed change
items: State the task problem, intended result and uncertainty.
Include relevant staff and community perspectives through usable routes.
Compare benefits, shifted burdens, requirements and evidence needs.

sections.heading: Make implementation workable
items: Name action owners, actual decision authority, resources and dependencies.
Prepare the changed task with usable information and practice.
Explain the change and maintain a responsible response route.
Keep urgent or formal matters out of routine waiting queues.

sections.heading: Review and follow through
items: Check the promised result with comparable evidence and privacy safeguards.
Separate observed differences from causal claims.
Connect supported next actions to the real implementation process and relevant ADSA goals.
Use consultant guidance while staff retain their work responsibility.
